pr_body:
Closes #10425

#### Changes

* Deprecate the boolean argument for `enable_string_cache`. The function now always enables the string cache.
* Add a new function `disable_string_cache`. This disables the string cache.
* Fix the implementation of the StringCache context manager.
* On the Rust side, rename `IUseStringCache` to `StringCacheHolder`. `IUse...` seemed like a weird name to me - but maybe I am missing some convention here.
* Some internal refactoring.

API is now consistent across the Rust and Python side - with the exception that Python offers a context manager instead of a RAII object.
pr_comments: Why two functions rather than one `use_string_cache(True | False`?

> Why two functions rather than one use_string_cache(True | False?

Some discussion on that in https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/8631 and in the linked issue.

I'm open to alternatives. But `use_string_cache` is confusable with `using_string_cache`. I like that the pair of functions `enable/disable` is super clear.
Alright, I don't have strong opinions about it.

`reset_` is being renamed to `disable_`. Maybe this change is to make the enable/disable symmetry more clear. However, this makes me realize that `enable_` here is a misnomer, as it increments the string cache counter. 

I'd rather call it something that reflects that action. `increment_string_cache_refcount` is what we do.

Basically, a few things can happen:
* Increment string cache refcount by 1
* Decrease string cache refcount by 1
* Set string cache refcount to 0
* Actually clear the string cache

The refcount is an implementation detail that we shouldn't show to users. So we have three functions:
* `enable_string_cache` - Turns on the cache. On the background, increases refcount by 1. But might as well increase it by 10, it doesn't really matter.
* `disable_string_cache` - Turns off the cache. Both sets refcount to 0 and clears the cache.
* Some context manager that enables the cache while its active. On the background, increases refcount by 1 on initialization and decreases by 1 when it's dropped.

This is what I implemented. I don't see a more user-friendly way to do this.

I think that we do need to document and make clear the implementation details as you can get race conditions. If a contextmanager (thread A) incremented the cache and another thread calls `disable_` (thread B), the program isn't correct anymore as the string cache was cleared under thread A's nose.

The way I see it, the global string cache isn't thread-safe anyway.

If one thread enables the global string cache, it will disrupt any other threads that are trying to construct local categoricals.

So I don't really get the discussion about thread safety, because it's not designed to be thread-safe (it's _global_...). But maybe I am misunderstanding things here.

We can add a warning somewhere in the docs to document this behavior, of course.

> So I don't really get the discussion about thread safety, because it's not designed to be thread-safe (it's _global_...). But maybe I am misunderstanding things here.

Sure, but enabling the string cache doesn't break a program, disabling does. We use the atomic reference counting to ensure a thread that holds the string cache will have the string cache for that lifetime. I think we must guarantee that, unless you call a very low level function like `disable_`/`reset_`, but I think the name of that function should stress that caveat.

We do atomic reference counting to ensure it is thread safe with regard to holding the string cache. 

> enable_string_cache - Turns on the cache. On the background, increases refcount by 1. But might as well increase it by 10, it doesn't really matter.

It does matter, as then the string cache will never get cleared. With the context manager and on the rust side the `StringCacheHolder` we ensure the string cache is cleared when everybody dropped their context.

@orlp Not sure how that extra boolean state would help matters here? Maybe we can discuss on Thursday.

Discussed the design with Ritchie at the office and I updated the PR with a warning that `disable_string_cache` is not thread safe. I think this can be merged and we can possibly improve thread-safety later with additional tech.
This PR is now done. @orlp mind reviewing to check if I implemented the pseudocode correctly?

issue_context.title: py-polars.enable_string_cache() does not simply turn on/off
issue_context.body:
### Checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.


### Reproducible example

```python
>>> import polars as pl
>>> pl.using_string_cache()
False
>>> pl.enable_string_cache(True)
>>> pl.enable_string_cache(True) # double-tap True
>>> pl.enable_string_cache(False)
>>> pl.using_string_cache()
True # NOT False !
>>> pl.enable_string_cache(False)  #double-tap False
>>> pl.using_string_cache()
False # now it is False
```


### Issue description

[in rust-polars ](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/c4ac8597b01725dd4d3562396bb5230ec3a71517/crates/polars-core/src/chunked_array/logical/categorical/stringcache.rs#L67) have some RAII approach to enable/disable. However this is not fully behavior-safe implemented reference counting, and each thread is required to only enable once and then disable to get reference counting right. The py-function has wrapped enable_string_cache() as if it was an on/off switch.

[in py-polars the docs simply states pl.enable_string_cache(toggle) is an on/off switch](https://pola-rs.github.io/polars/py-polars/html/reference/api/polars.enable_string_cache.html#polars-enable-string-cache)

maybe enable_string_cache() should not be a public function as it has global side effects, and any use should go
through `IUseStringCache`which is probably the RAII behaviour-safe version intended for use.



### Expected behavior

It depends, but if pl.enable_string_cache(toggle) should be a simple on/off  switch, then 

```python
>>> import polars as pl
>>> pl.using_string_cache()
False
>>> pl.enable_string_cache(True)
>>> pl.enable_string_cache(True)
>>> pl.enable_string_cache(False)
>>> pl.using_string_cache()
False
```

comments: I think we should document remove boolean the argument. That way you can only turn it on, or use the context manager, which is RAII.

Yeah, I mentioned in #8631 that it seems awkward having "enable" and "True" together, it feels redundant. If the boolean does something, the function should be named `set_string_cache(True|False)`, or the boolean should be removed entirely.

@mcrumiller  I agree `set_string_cache()` would be a better name for a switch, but under the hood it is[ actually a reference counter](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/c4ac8597b01725dd4d3562396bb5230ec3a71517/crates/polars-core/src/chunked_array/logical/categorical/stringcache.rs#L67). Above zero means someone somewhere still thinks the string_cache should be active.

It could be `enable_string_cache()` only can do +1 and thereby forces the string_cache always stay "on".
But then also exposing the public rust function `reset_string_cache()` which brings the counter to zero and cleans up. 

Then documentation should warn the user these on/off functions are very crude, and advice the user to prefer any context_manager like `with_string_cache()` or a function-decorator or similar.
Yes, I think we should call it enable and expose a reset. Care to make a PR?
I will check in on this issue in a week when I return from vacation :)

So out of curiosity, does each `with pl.StringCache()` context have its own cache, or is it that a series uses its own string cache or the global one?

Edit: from testing, looks like it's the former. I'm a bit confused now, it seems like:

1. You can use enable a "global" string cache, shared by all categoricals that are made after this is enabled;
2. You can use a context manager, in which case all strings within that manager use their own isolated string cache; or
3. You can use nothing, in which case a series will have its own string mapping and nobody else can interact with it.

Is the "global" string cache a special cache compared to those created with a context manager?

As long as the string cache is getting revisited, does it make sense to introduce an environment variable like POLARS_STRING_CACHE_ENABLED that, when set to True at import time would turn the global string cache on?

I know there has been some contention between people wanting it always on so they don't have to explicitly turn it on and people who don't want to keep seeing questions about joins not working against those who want max performance by default.

I am ambivalent on the default debate but the environment variable approach seems like it'd appease everyone.

@deanm0000, while I'm in the camp of wanting to always using the global string cache, I don't like the idea of an environmental variable that changes actual behavior of polars. Env vars should change *how* polars does operations (e.g. prevent partitioning, or changing print behavior), but IMO it shouldn't change *what* polars does. This could lead to really annoying reproducibility problems: if someone else runs the exact same code, there's not even the *expectation* that it will run the same.
I apologize for unmet promises. I have changed job and cannot for time being contribute.
No problem at all, of course. Good luck with the new job!

review_comments:
Pretty sure this is race condition. Someone could have already incremented the `STRING_CACHE_REFCOUNT` again and used it in the meantime, and now we clear it.

I think we should just wrap the `STRING_CACHE_REFCOUNT` in a mutex, and then hold the mutex while clearing the cache.

It's not like we increment/decrement the string cache refcount so often that an atomic is really necessary here.
Yeah this code seemed questionable to me too (it was already there). I can take another look and refactor this in one go, thanks for the suggestion!
Implemented as a mutex now, is this what you had in mind @orlp ?
